t: Your Brain Is Rotting: A Leadership Survival Guide
q: The human brain evolved for bursts of decision-making, not for 50+ decisions a day. It wasn't designed to handle a dozen tabs open, three simultaneous chat threads, constant notifications, and back-to-back Zoom meetings.

A study by McKinsey found that the average knowledge worker spends 62% of their time on “work about work”: meetings, email, coordination. Only 27% goes to actual skilled work, and a mere 11% to strategy or innovation. That's right. As a leader, you spend less than 3 hours a week on deep, creative, strategic thinking, the kind of thinking that moves your team forward.

When your brain is overloaded: Your memory fades. Your mood dips. You get reactive, not proactive. You avoid hard problems. You fall back on habits and familiar routines. Which means your leadership becomes… hollow.

You start to feel like a slightly worse version of yourself every week. It's not enough to crash, but just enough to coast. Until one day you wake up and realize: I haven't felt fully alive at work in months.

Most leaders don't recognize the problem, so they reach for the wrong fixes. … These are the equivalent of putting ice cubes in a burning room, hoping the room cools down. It won't. More tools won't save your brain from rotting. Less noise will.

I've found that the best ideas don't come when I'm sitting in front of my computer or browsing my phone. They come when my mind wanders. When I go for a walk (without my phone), in the shower, or when I'm lying down in bed. Studies from neuroscience (e.g., the DMN: Default Mode Network) show that the brain becomes more creative, reflective, and emotionally insightful when it's not focused on a task.
If an athlete ran 12 hours a day with no rest, what would you call him? Most will call him reckless. But when we, as leaders, run our brains to the extreme every week, we call it “drive.

Your edge as a leader isn't how much you do. It's how clearly you think. It's how calmly you decide. It's how creatively you solve problems. And none of that is possible if you allow your brain to rot under the noise and the pressure.” Archived from The Good Boss on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

q: My answer to this question in almost every context and for almost every student is the same; “Use The Point Game!” The Point Game is a cornerstone of Evidence-Based Literacy Instruction's (EBLI) approach to motivation and behavior reinforcement during instruction, whether in the whole class setting or 1:1.

Here's how it works: the instructor assigns a number of points for executing a particular skill independently, accurately, or correctly. If the student can demonstrate a skill, they earn X number of points. The teacher records their points in a T chart labeled Teacher v. Student.

Playing The Point Game presents an opportunity to build or break trust with students. Inevitably, you will be confronted with unexpected situations around earning points. In these moments, it is important to be honest about how many points you give for certain things and to demonstrate follow-through.

Taking away points is unnecessarily punitive, breaks trust with students, and complicates the mathematical function of The Point Game. Instead of taking away points, just give yourself points when the student does something that you want to reinforce against.

Give students the chance to earn large sums of points for hard tasks. Breaking a guessing habit, learning to use an “ice skater” finger underneath words while reading when they realllllllyyyy want to tap their finger across the page, keeping one's gaze fixed on a word while decoding instead of looking up at the teacher, these things are really difficult for students to implement, especially when it means fighting a strongly held habit.

Many teachers fall into the trap of never giving themselves any points, allowing the students points to stack up and surrendering, “you beat me, I didn't get a single one!” Over time, this will weaken the effectiveness of The Point Game because there is no real competition.

When I get points for students doing something they shouldn't, I clearly explain my rationale and then I give them a chance to try again, which might sound something like this; “I'm getting a point because you didn't form the letter F the way we practiced, with a hook around then cross. If you can do it right in the next word, you can get 5 points.

Wrap up each session by counting up the students points. This may be a moment to practice skip counting or multi-digit addition. It may be a moment to call out the hard work students did during the session, or remind them of something they learned and to practice those same strategies when reading independently.” Archived from Science of Reading Classroom on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Learning Science of Deep Processing
q: Shallow processing involves focusing on attributes that remain on the surface or the look-alike of what you want to learn (typically at the visual or sound levels), such as the appearance or pronunciation of words. It also refers to engaging in rote activities that reinforce those superficial aspects like repetition, rereading and highlighting.

Concentration is about attention. It's the ability to sustain focus and resist distraction. Deep processing is about what you do with that focus. You can concentrate intensely on a shallow task. Anyone who has ever memorized a list word for word knows this feeling. It takes effort. It feels demanding. And yet the information often disappears quickly.

A recent study showed that simply asking students “why?” after introducing new information made them remember that information incredibly better. The reason is elaborative interrogation: studies show that students who generate explanations remember more and transfer knowledge better than those who simply read explanations.

Research shows that relating information to yourself provides a powerful scaffold to organize information, not just emotional relevance. In practice, this means that tying information to personal experiences, goals or beliefs helps encoding by making it feel relevant to one's own life.

Short learning bursts feel faster, but they can slow down the path to durable understanding when they prevent deep engagement. Ironically, learners often reach long-term retention sooner by spending time processing meaning deeply than by spreading attention thin across many brief sessions.

Efficiency in learning is not necessarily about shorter exposure. It's about doing the right kind of thinking for the right amount of time and, paradoxically, that often means “for long enough”.” Archived from Kognitivo on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How to Think Like a Leader Before You Feel Like One
q: Early in my career I felt that credibility came from speed and execution. Clients asked a question; I raced to answer. Teams brought a problem; I offered a fix. As I took on leadership roles, I realised that (1) I didn't have time to be a doer in the same way; and (2) it was no longer my job to do so! Instead of acting and effectively closing spaces that others could own, I had to provide the space for others to think for themselves.

My natural instinct was (and still is!) to sketch a solution. Instead, I asked, “What would success look like if we got this right?” The room went quiet for a few seconds. Then, ideas started to surface: hesitant at first, then layered and richer. Within twenty minutes they had built a vision none of us could have produced alone.
Holding a question like in this example doesn't mean being evasive or lacking confidence. It means resisting the reflex to perform knowledge and instead creating a space for shared sense-making.

When I first stepped into leadership roles, I thought the job was to push. Push projects forward, push performance, push for change. It took me a while to realise that most people and teams actually struggle because something is slowing them down.

Leadership, I've learned, is often about identifying and removing these hidden barriers. You can spot them by paying attention to what hinders colleagues: unclear roles, competing expectations, unspoken conflict, fragmented processes, interpersonal tensions that people are worried they can't voice.

One of the hardest transitions in leadership is realising that your internal weather becomes everyone else's climate. You may think you're having a private moment of frustration, but people feel the shift instantly. Tone, posture, speed of speech — teams track these cues far more than we imagine.

My irritation didn't stay contained. It set the emotional baseline, and the meeting shifted toward managing the tension I had brought into the room. We spent the next hour dealing with the consequences of a mood swing rather than the substance of the work.

A leadership mindset is the craft of shaping the conditions under which good thinking, good work and good relationships can emerge. … Together, these practices shift leadership from performance to stewardship: you are not trying to be impressive, but to be useful.” Archived from Andrea Chiarelli on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How Do I Hold My People Accountable?
q: How do I hold my people accountable?” is the #1 question I get from the CEOs I teach. The answer is relatively simple, but it's not easy and it requires a pretty involved process.

The accountability process begins before you ever hire someone. It starts with you answering two questions: What job needs to be done? Who fits that role best? Making sure your hire has the right aptitude and motivation is critical. You can't hold someone accountable for work they don't have the skills to perform or the motivation to engage in.” “Once you've hired the right person, the next step in the accountability process is micro-training. Too many businesses skip this entirely, then act surprised when the new hire doesn't do things the way they want.
Now, you need to document their responsibilities and key metrics in what I call an Executive Performance Profile. This step, too, gets skipped or glossed over all the time, but it's essential.
At these meetings, ask each employee: “How likely are you to achieve these goals on time?” Notice we're asking for a prediction, not a progress report. This may seem subtle, but it's crucial.

If you let employees just feed you data, “Hey boss, I'm 10% done… 20% done… 50% done”, they're not taking accountability for delivering the result. They're just reporting progress, which means you're the one ultimately accountable.
There are good reasons a goal might not be achieved. But there are very few good reasons someone didn't know they weren't going to achieve it.

The main thing I want to communicate here is that so many managers (CEOs included) jump straight to the accountability conversation without laying this foundation. That's unfair to the employee and to the organization. … That works a hell of a lot better than hire → hope → retaliate.” Archived from Managing the Future on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Fred Rogers, the Teaching Mentor
q: While competitors ran animated features, Rogers stuck to physical sets and puppeteering. While “best practice” in children's television programming shifted to graphics and variety and speed and novelty, Rogers started every show walking onto the same old set and following the same old ritual: song, jacket, cardigan, shoes.
Too often, what we call “best practice” is really just “new” or “popularly accepted” or “endorsed by a guru.

The term “best practice” gets thrown around a lot, and it makes sense: we're all after “what's best for kids” and, therefore, we want to be doing the “best practices” possible for getting after that best. The trouble with this term, however, is that it's become over-extended.

Educators have got to have minds and hearts and souls that deeply understand how students work, how learning works, and how basic teacher moves can help students learn. With deep understanding in place, we're able to develop classrooms that look simple, even laughably so, like Rogers', yet produce consistent and profound results.
Good, timeless, well-founded practice > what passes as “best practice” these days.

Rogers seems to have been an expert at the internal work of teaching. The learning, the understanding, the processing. His clarity of thought, his obvious goodness, his simplicity of practice, his deep humility: these were the natural results of discipline and reflection, not luck or genetics or talent.

He understood himself. He understood his neighbor. He was a student of what it means to be a human being. (And no, not everyone is.) Such apprenticeship must be first intended and then sought; you don't accidentally stumble upon it.

Rogers knew he didn't control the circumstances of the world. He couldn't change the attention-hungry changes in children's programs. He just controlled his program, his teaching. He contented himself in that, worked at doing good through that for a full career, and his legacy speaks for itself.” Archived from Dave Stuart Jr. newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Close the Tabs: An End of Term Ritual for School Leaders
q: As the autumn term winds down and we head towards the Christmas break, school leaders often find themselves carrying far more than festive cheer into the holidays. We often carry open loops — the mental “tabs” that never seem to close.

It's strangely common: the people we line manage often get the least of our time. Urgent parent emails, safeguarding triage, assessment deadlines…these soak up the hours. Meanwhile, your competent, dependable team members quietly keep everything afloat.

Ah, the last-minute paperwork. The document you meant to submit. The file you intended to upload. The resource you promised to send “later today.” These are the things that wake us at 3am on Christmas Eve, demanding attention from the depths of our subconscious.” “You don't need to solve these before Christmas. But you do need to name them. Write each worry on a piece of paper, just the problem, not the solution. Allow it to live there instead of in your mind. Let the page hold it over Christmas so that your brain doesn't have to.
January can feel like a cold plunge if the first week back hasn't been thought about in advance.

At the end of a long term, patterns reveal themselves. Perhaps you've particularly noticed: rising stress, recurring disorganisation, a structural issue in your school, a creeping sense of overwhelm. So ask: What words, ideas or emotions do I want the New Year to hold?

It has been a long term. Students are tired. Behaviour dips. Emotions run high. And sometimes the things students say or do can sit heavy with us long after the moment has passed. But remember the mantra: They are the children. We are the adults.
Close the tabs you can. Write down the ones you can't, and walk into the holiday knowing you have earned every moment of rest.” Archived from Language for Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Grading Teacher Performance Kills Growth
q: When I started my teacher training over ten years ago, I faced a series of challenges like the relentless planning burden and subpar mentoring among them. But there was another element that amplified my anxiety to levels I haven’t fully recovered from: the lesson grading system.

A 60-minute snapshot of a teacher managing a highly complex concept with a challenging class is reduced to a single word. This grade carries zero context about the teacher’s long-term planning, their mastery of instructional atoms, or their relationships with the students.
When you grade, you ruin the positivity of the process and shift the focus from growth to judgment.

t: When a Team Member Doesn't Prioritize Your Priorities
q: Sometimes unknowingly and other times deliberately, team members can follow their own priorities and fail to follow yours. This can be a source of great frustration for leaders, as the work they want to get done takes a secondary position or, worse, gets ignored.
Leaders faced with the challenge of a team member who ignores their priorities are best served by initially NOT presuming bad intent.

It’s possible the team member has received competing priorities from other leaders; they are simply overloaded, and it only appears they are avoiding the priorities. Or, perhaps, they don’t understand the priority set.” “In the case where the root cause is not obvious to the team member, or they are unwilling to share it, the leader needs to make one point perfectly clear: the priorities they set are non-negotiable. This means the team member’s evaluation and success depend on their accomplishing them.
By connecting the priorities to the team’s vision, purpose, or long-range goals, the leader can further imprint the consequences of placing anything ahead of the priorities.

By plainly naming the refusal and avoiding any debate over the priorities, the leader must act decisively to define the role the team member is asked to play and to offer them a clear choice to accept the role or exit the team.
Effectiveness in anything is about doing the right things. Leaders set priorities to make the team more effective. If someone can’t or won’t align with those priorities, trust gets broken.
As author Jim Collins likes to say, “The moment you feel the need to tightly manage someone, you likely have the wrong person.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: So Much We Do, We Do Again (Resuscitating Repetition)
q: They say that writing is rewriting and that good reading is rereading. The wisdom we have inherited tells us again and again — or repeats for us — that anything mastered is done not once but many, many times.

Quintilian tells us, “It is better to learn a little thoroughly and to repeat it often, than to learn much superficially.” Jerome writes, “Constant repetition is the mother of studies” and Seneca says simply “let us repeat often what we have learned.

Rightly conceived, repetition is a very good and human thing. We employ it to learn, perform, and enjoy music; we learn it to dance, play tennis, and make a good old-fashioned. Children understand innately the virtue of repetition and even demand it: Read it again Daddy! One more time!

The root of this Latinate word is instructive — for it means to petition or seek…again. There are many good things to seek in life, worth seeking and finding over and over again, whether a great concert, a great drink, or a great book.

Of course there is a kind of repetition employed in education (and in other aspects of life) that merits the description “drill and kill” and “rote memory.” To seek again, to repeat, is deeply human and good thing. But anything good can be corrupted, and we corrupt the good of repetition repeatedly.

It is possible to review the causes for the Revolutionary War in a way that is dull and uninspiring (a regurgitation or retreading). Dull teachers do this regularly. But it is also possible to review (revisit, reconsider, remark, return, relive) the cause of the war in ways that are remarkable, refreshing, and renewing.
Much depends on which verb you wish to attach the sacred prefix.

Much of bad teaching is bad repetition that equates to test prep. t: Combining Student Scores: Why Adding Subjects Is Trickier Than It Looks
q: One example that Paul shared with me really got me thinking about what happens when we add scores from different subjects.

If we have a group of 12 students, and have their percentage scores on 8 subjects, it might seem easy to work out who is the best students. We just add up the scores on each of the 8 subjects, and see who has the highest total.
However, there is a problem here. Subject 1 used most of the mark range, with scores ranging from 10 to 100, while others, such as subject 3, have scores ranging only from 40 to 60.
To control for this, we could replace scores with class ranks, giving the highest scoring student in each subject a rank of 1, and the lowest scoring student a rank of 12.
However, when we use ranks, we throw away information, because we take no account of how much better the first ranked student is than the lowest ranked student; the difference will always be 11.

Instead, a better approach might be to scale the scores so that every subject uses the full range of scores from 0 to 100, with the lowest scoring student getting 0, the highest scoring student getting 100, and the others scaled in between.
Now, the student who was top — Adams — is at the bottom, and the student who was at the bottom — Lant — is at the top.
If that doesn’t make you realize that adding up scores like this is not as straightforward as it seems, I don’t know what will.” Archived from Dylan Wiliam on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Case for Saying Less
q: When people don’t understand, explaining more usually makes it worse.
When someone looks confused, we assume the problem is a lack of explanation. That assumption is usually wrong. It’s a habit built over years of good intentions.

Controlled experiments in cognitive science point to a quieter truth. When researchers gave people additional explanations they believed would help, comprehension actually declined. Not slightly. Reliably.” “The issue wasn’t intelligence or motivation. It was capacity. Working memory is limited. When it’s flooded, the brain shifts from understanding to coping.
When unnecessary information is removed, understanding improves. People make better decisions because they can grasp the core more quickly.

t: Professional Scepticism
q: Until education becomes the kind of profession that reveres evidence, we should not be surprised to find its experts dispensing unproven methods, endlessly flitting from one fad to another. The greatest victims of these fads are the very students who are most at risk.
Science can help us understand what is. It is far less helpful when it comes to deciding what ought to be. Facts about the world do not contain values hidden inside them, waiting to be discovered.

To be professional sceptical is to engage in the disciplined habit of questioning claims by asking what evidence supports them, how that evidence was generated, and what would count against the claim being true.

We are not neutral judges of our own ideas. We are inclined to defend beliefs we have invested time, effort or reputation in. We discount evidence that challenges us and overvalue evidence that confirms what we already think.

t: Onions: What Understanding Actually Means
q: What do we mean when we say a pupil “understands” something? The word is doing an astonishing amount of work in classrooms, and most of the time we don’t notice that it is.

A pupil who can follow the procedure and produce the grid understands something. t: How I Trained My Memory, and What It Taught Me About Learning
q: I spent several months training myself to memorise 100 random digits in five minutes. It worked. I can now do it, most days. But the interesting thing is not the result. The interesting thing is what the training revealed about how learning works.

The headline skill — memorise 100 digits in 5 minutes — is emergent. It’s made up of component skills you practise separately, the way a pianist practises scales, chord shifts, and sight-reading before ever playing a piece.
Small chunks beat large ones. Every time I tried to process more than a few digits at a time, my accuracy collapsed. Every time I stuck to the two-digit chunk the PAO system uses, I was fine.
The connection is everything. The vivid, often absurd story linking one image to the next is what makes retrieval possible at speed. A bland connection is a broken connection.
Varied practice beat repetitive practice. The days I mixed in different digit sequences, different starting points, different distractions, I got better faster than the days I drilled the same thing.

Effortful retrieval is where the durable learning lives. The moment a recall felt easy, I was usually about to get it wrong the next time. The moment it felt hard, I was usually about to strengthen it.

Distraction has a measurable cost. I could see it in my own timings, reliably, before I could feel it subjectively. Five seconds of checking a phone cost me ten seconds of recall speed on the next attempt.

Transfer is narrower than it feels. Getting better at memorising digits did not make me better at remembering names, or facts in a meeting. Transfer is a skill you have to build on purpose; it does not come free with practice.” Archived from fivetwelvethirteen on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Got Regrets Yet? Teachers and the Four Types of Regret
q: Regret isn’t just a rumination. Used well, it’s a source of information. It tells us what we value, what we wish we had done differently, and, most usefully, what we want to do now.
Dan Pink, in his book The Power of Regret, identifies four types of regret that cut across cultures: Foundation regrets, Boldness regrets, Moral regrets, and Connection regrets.

Foundation regrets come from failing to do the slow, unglamorous work that sets a person up for long-term flourishing. For teachers, this often looks like systems not built, habits not formed, subject expertise not deepened.

Boldness regrets come from playing it safe when a braver choice was available. For teachers, this might mean the unit we didn’t try, the discussion we chickened out of, the project we shrank to fit our comfort zone.
Moral regrets come from moments when we acted against our values, even briefly. A sharp word to a struggling student, a rushed judgment in a parent email, a corner cut on a colleague who needed us.

Connection regrets come from relationships left unattended. The student we never quite got through to, the co-worker we meant to thank, the kid who slipped through the cracks while we were busy with the louder ones.
Pink offers a simple three-step process: relive the regret briefly, reframe it as information about what you value, then extract and apply a single concrete change.

Our regrets, handled well, become the coordinates for the next chapter. They point us toward the Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging we most want to build next.” Archived from Dave Stuart Jr. on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Missing the Wood for the Trees
q: The claim that domain-adjacent prior knowledge does not support new in-domain learning looks, at first glance, like a body-blow to one of the most widely quoted maxims in educational psychology. If “the most important factor in learning is what students already know,” how can a new experimental study report that supplying domain-related knowledge makes no difference at all?

If this looks uncannily like the result reported by Buchin and Mulligan, that’s because both studies hinge on the same conceptual mistake. They assume that any increase in knowledge should automatically produce gains on any chosen assessment.

t: Are Your People Trained Or Enabled?
q: Organizations invest billions annually in developing their workforce, yet many struggle to translate learning investments into durable performance improvements. At the heart of this challenge rests a fundamental distinction that is often overlooked: the difference between training your people and enabling your people.

Good training asks the question: “What do people need to know and understand to be able to do their jobs more effectively?” It operates on a push model. The organization decides what, when, and how learning happens.

Enablement, by contrast, is continuous and context-embedded. It requires an ecosystem of resources, tools, processes, and support systems that help people perform effectively in their daily workflows. Enablement asks: “What do people need to succeed, and how can we provide it when they need it?
I tend to think of training like an fancy appetizer at an overpriced restaurant. I mean, we kind of need it to get going, but it’s not nearly enough to satisfy and sustain us.
The distinction between training and enablement matters not just because people want and need support in the moment, but because knowledge transfer alone rarely produces lasting behavioral change.

Training and learning industry professionals generally agree that learners are likely to forget approximately 70% of training content within 24 hours and up to 90% within a week. This is supported by the concept of the forgetting curve, first documented by psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, which shows that without reinforcement, memory retention decays.

Training can promote dependency and even disempowerment, as people are adapted to leaning into a particular kind of person or setting for learning rather than seek it out in everyday moments. Enablement, on the other hand, empowers people to solve problems with greater autonomy.

t: The Double Diamond
q: NASA was once exploring ways to keep astronauts fit during long space missions. Someone on the NASA team floated an idea that became an instant hit: Send a Peloton bike into space. It sounded wild at first, but not totally unreasonable.

But then, just as this idea was gaining traction, someone on the team asked a different question: What’s the problem we’re trying to solve? Or, put another way, “Are we trying to send a bike into orbit? Or are we trying to keep astronauts healthy in zero gravity?

That simple shift in perspective changed how NASA approached this. Eventually, instead of a heavy, expensive, over-engineered bike, the solution turned out to be, wait for it, a resistance band. Cheap, light and effective.
Fundamentally, what the astronauts really needed wasn’t a bike. They needed fitness, and that needed tension, which could be delivered through a simple resistance band.

As leaders, that’s the trap that most of us fall into at work. We chase “clever” fixes, and sometimes fail to identify the “real” problem. We jump at solutions before we identify the problem we’re trying to solve.

Sometimes, the hardest part of leadership isn’t solving the problem, it’s knowing what the problem actually is. The Double Diamond gives you a way to zoom out before you zoom in. It helps you to look at the full picture, not just the part that’s loudest or most visible.

At its core, it helps you separate two things most teams blur together: The problem space: where you slow down, explore, and figure out what’s really going wrong. The solution space: where you start thinking about how to fix it.

The Double Diamond works in four stages: Discover: explore the problem from all angles. Define: identify the real problem worth solving. Develop: explore possible solutions. Deliver: test and launch the best one.” Archived from The Good Boss on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Stop Guessing. Measure Your Maths Instruction.
q: Most conversations about improving maths instruction begin with assumptions. We assume certain routines are in place, that modelling is clear or that students are getting enough practice. In reality, improvement starts when we stop guessing and describe what is actually happening in classrooms.

One of the most persistent problems in school improvement is that decisions are often made before the problem is properly described. Professional learning is selected, programs are adopted and new practices are introduced without a clear understanding of what is actually happening in classrooms.

When the need is externally defined, goals belong to others. Teachers are asked to engage with ideas without first understanding why they matter or how they connect to their own practice. Engagement becomes optional, resistance becomes understandable and change remains shallow.

Research consistently shows that professional learning has the greatest impact when it is tightly focused on specific challenges, grounded in classroom evidence and linked directly to student outcomes rather than abstract principles (Antoniou et al., 2015; Timperley et al., 2008).

Improvement does not start with choosing what to do next. It starts with accurately describing what is happening now. Without that clarity, even well intentioned decisions are unlikely to lead to meaningful change.

What matters is not the total score itself. What matters is what the score makes visible. The descriptors provide a common reference point. Instead of debating whether modelling is “good enough”, leaders can point to specific indicators that describe what modelling actually looks like at different levels of quality.

The end of the year is rarely the right moment to introduce new initiatives. It is, however, the ideal time to take stock. Completing the scorecard now allows leadership teams to step back from day to day pressures and look for patterns.

If you are planning for next year, start with restraint. Measure before you modify. Describe before you decide. Choose one priority that genuinely matters. Improvement does not begin with new initiatives. It begins with clarity.” Archived from Knowledge for Teachers on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Stop Adding & Start Improving
q: I took a genuine interest in the research behind it, which led me to publicly present on checks for understanding in early 2023, and it is woven through my current research studies. Even this year, at researchED Ballarat, I presented on responsive maths teaching (essentially checks for understanding in a mathematics context) and sat in Bron Ryrie-Jones’ brilliant session on the very same topic on the same day.

From the outside, that might look a little obsessive. It might seem unusual to sit in on a session about something you teach and research yourself. But that is precisely the point. I walked away from Bron’s session with pages of notes, fresh ways of thinking and ideas I had not considered. Expertise does not exempt us from learning. If anything, it increases our responsibility to keep refining.

Schools often treat professional learning just like a menu though. We choose the topic of the term, taste it briefly and then move onto a new topic with good marketing. The problem is, even for topics that do yield greater progress for students or are effective in achieving their aims, expertise doesn’t sufficiently development from tasting.

Often teacher resistance is seen as being one of the biggest barriers to school change, but I’d posit that leadership impatience is a far bigger barrier. Schools are often so eager to demonstrate momentum with new initiatives, complete with flashy social media marketing, that they equate exposure with progress.

It isn’t uncommon for schools to abandon an initiative after a term to either move onto the next popular thing or because somehow 2 months wasn’t enough time to totally transform results. The only result of this is initiative fatigue for staff. Teachers aren’t given the opportunity to become experts because they are rarely given the time or support to refine their work to the point of mastery.

School improvement can certainly be a knowledge problem, but it’s also a conditions problem. Rather than exposure to more ideas, staff need time to move a little deeper than surface level on the existing ideas that evidence tells us works. This means time, feedback, repetition and accountability to refine the techniques that matter.

Teachers aren’t afraid of improvement. We’re exhausted by shiny popular instructional techniques that continually reappear with a new name like a trend that just won’t die. The truth of it is though that you can be a brilliant teacher and be brilliant at implementing a technique, but still have room to sharpen it.

Schools that make real impact aren’t about chasing novelty. They double down on what works and refuse to move until it has teeth. t: AI Isn't The Problem. Your Decisions Are.
q: There’s a thing called the Iceberg of Ignorance. It says that senior leadership only knows 4% of a company’s problems. Frontline workers know 100% of them. Yet it’s these same senior leaders who are making the big strategic decisions for companies, despite the fact they only know 4% of the problems.

Company leaders are treating AI as a solution, even though nobody has defined the problem. AI has become the corporate version of the flashy red Mustang in a mid-life crisis. But adding AI because “everyone else is doing it” is not innovation, that’s more like Halloween. Just because you’re dressed as a superhero, doesn’t mean you will fly.

When a company starts with the solution instead of the problem, there are five predictable pitfalls: They automate the wrong thing. They create more work instead of less. They break processes that weren’t broken. They confuse and overwhelm employees. They waste money and morale. Simply put, if you automate chaos, all you’re gonna end up with is more chaos.

Real problems have four specific characteristics: Pain: People are feeling pain (it’s not just execs with FOMO). Cost: You can measure the real cost of not implementing a solution. Problem: The people impacted by the problem can describe it in one sentence. Improvement: Solving the problem will quickly improve efficiency, revenue and sanity.
Our customer support team is drowning in tickets” is a real problem that needs fixing. “Our competitors are moving faster with AI” is not.

They abandoned their roadmap, rerouted resources, and built an AI product in six weeks. They lost three clients because they failed to deliver on promises. Because they ignored fixing the tech debt, the AI performs inconsistently, at best. The clients that tried it don’t understand why they need it and asked for it to be removed. Team morale has sunk lower than low.

If you think you’re putting the solution before the problem, here is a simple 3-question framework to keep you in check. What human pain are we trying to solve? What would success look like without AI? Is AI the simplest and most effective way to solve this, or is it just the coolest? If you can’t answer all three, you’re not solving a problem. You’re probably creating one.

The future doesn’t belong to the companies that adopt AI the fastest. It belongs to the companies that adopt AI the wisest. AI isn’t the threat. AI isn’t the enemy. AI isn’t coming for your job. Your poor decision-making is. So start with the problem. End with the tool.” Archived from The Best Leadership Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

Although they appeared more prepared than ever before, detailed note sheets covered with text, in reality many could not articulate a coherent response in the face of any kind of rebuttal.

In fall 2025, within minutes of opening an LLM, any MS student with even rudimentary prompting skills can generate a sophisticated case with solid arguments, detailed evidence, and clear structure. The AI will anticipate counterarguments and provide rebuttals.

While creating cases is exactly what debate preparation is supposed to produce, the process is supposed to take weeks, the result of hard work and earned knowledge. When there’s literally no effort required to generate detailed arguments, all the worst aspects of using AI come into play.

What I observed across multiple rounds Saturday was striking sameness. Almost all the arguments were identical, the same three points on each side, the same evidence cited, the same structure, because it was all being drawn from the same pool of training data.

That’s why I think public speaking activities, debate, Model UN, mock trial, speech competitions, will become increasingly valuable as AI continues to transform education. t: Good Leaders Explain the Logic Behind Their Everyday Beliefs
q: Observe great leaders in action, and you will frequently hear them use simple statements that justify their beliefs with evidence, facts, and data. Brian Gottlieb, former CEO and the author of Beyond the Hammer, calls these expressions Belief-Because statements. These evidence-based affirmations pair a core belief with a specific “because” rationale.

This is my preferred candidate because their skills match the role perfectly.” “We should pause the project because the risk assessment now shows a high probability of failure.” “We must enter the mid-market segment because our customer research shows unmet demand.

By aligning the leader’s beliefs with proven outcomes, Belief-Because statements often produce an echo of support and conviction. People like to repeat the rationale leaders offer. This makes any proposal or assertion easier to accept.

t: The Unique Challenge of Leading in a Matrix Organization
q: In a matrix organization, team members report to more than one leader or manager at the same time, typically a functional leader and a business or regional leader. This creates a grid-like system of accountability instead of a single straight line of reporting.

A Weak Matrix is where the functional leader dominates, and the project or daily task leader has limited authority. A Strong Matrix is where the project leader has primary authority and the functional leader mainly manages strategy and resource allocation. In a Balanced Matrix, the functional and project leaders share authority relatively equally.

Leading in a matrix organization requires a stronger emphasis on influence, collaboration, and negotiation than a traditional hierarchy. Because leaders share people, decisions, and resources with other leaders, they must resolve conflicting priorities with peers directly.

Success often depends on influencing without authority, negotiating tradeoffs, and securing buy-in from people who do not formally report to the leader. The impact of decisions on other functions, regions, and projects must always take precedence over simply making a call.

Instead of dictating solutions to problems, leaders in a matrix must learn to guide the group to decisions. It takes political and organizational savvy to navigate the formal and informal power structures that reside in the matrix.

Of the many influence strategies critical to effective leadership in a matrix organization, informational power stands out. By gathering and sharing information, leaders show themselves to be credible sources and important to others’ success. Unlike expert power (based on skill) or authority power (based on position), informational power comes from having access to valuable information and using it effectively.

Good leaders in a matrix share information to build trust by explaining the why behind their requests, reducing uncertainty by offering timely updates, presenting data in a way that highlights the benefits of a proposed action, gathering data and evidence to support a plan or strategy, offering insights and perspectives to increase buy-in, and marshaling benchmarks and metrics to make a convincing case.

t: The Myth of Teaching Children to ‘Read for Pleasure’
q: Although reading for pleasure has become one of education’s unassailable goods, the case for it is not quite as simple as we sometimes pretend. Over the past decade the rhetoric has drifted a long way from the evidence. We repeat slogans as if they were truths: children who read more do better; enjoyment drives attainment; make reading enjoyable and the results will follow. The trouble is that these claims don’t really survive contact with what the best studies actually show.

The leap from correlation to causation is far less certain. Much of the effect appears to flow in the opposite direction: stronger readers tend to enjoy reading more. Fluency produces pleasure rather than pleasure producing fluency. The idea that enjoyment is the engine of achievement has always been more wishful than evidential.

The shift from sustained prose to rapid, novelty-driven browsing appears to make the act of reading feel slow and effortful by comparison. Repeated exposure to fast, fragmentary content raises the threshold at which slower cognitive activities feel engaging. In effect, reading loses its grip because the mind has been conditioned to expect constant stimulation.

In this climate, school strategies that promise to “make reading fun” often ring hollow. They assume reading must compete with TikTok or YouTube on the same terrain. Yet the more reading is framed as entertainment, the more it is judged by entertainment’s standards. When a novel is set against a feed that updates every second, it is hardly surprising that it loses.

What stronger readers accumulate is not just volume but difficulty. They tend to choose continuous narrative and expository prose with enough syntactic and conceptual stretch to deepen comprehension. In other words, they read the kind of texts that do the cognitive heavy lifting.

Children who stick to very simple books, graphic hybrids or short conversational texts may accumulate volume without any substantial gain in their capacity to handle complex prose. The reading diet looks healthy only if you ignore the nutrients.

Skilled readers tend to choose books with enough challenge to build vocabulary and inferential skill. Weaker readers retreat to comfort: texts with predictable syntax, familiar topics and minimal cognitive demand. The result is that autonomy amplifies existing differences rather than equalising them.

Reading for pleasure is good, but not because it magically transforms struggling readers into keen ones. It is good because reading can only become pleasurable once it stops being painfully hard. Pleasure is a lagging indicator of fluency. Schools cannot shortcut this by sprinkling cushions, offering biscuits or running competitions. They can only do the slow work of teaching children to read with accuracy and stamina so that books open rather than resist.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: In Search of a Foundation for Disciplinary AI Literacy
q: Disciplines are strange objects. They have mass, weight, institutional presence. We build departments around them, hire into them, defend dissertations within their boundaries. And yet, observed closely, they blur. The edges soften. What looked like a unified field of practice reveals itself as swarms of competing methods, conflicting epistemologies, practitioners who barely recognize each other’s work as belonging to the same endeavor.

History is real. But what is historical thinking? Stand far enough back and it coheres: archives, evidence, argument, interpretation. Move closer and it dissolves into genealogies, microhistories, quantitative social science, intellectual history, each operating with different assumptions about what counts as a fact and how we come to know the past.

Yet students need something to work with. Teachers need frameworks that function on Tuesday morning. K-12 education cannot wait for disciplines to resolve their internal debates, because those debates are constitutive of what disciplines are. The argument is the discipline.

We talk about “the scientific method” as though it’s a settled procedure, a series of steps any scientist would recognize. But working scientists don’t follow a universal method. A field biologist, a particle physicist, and a clinical researcher operate with radically different practices, constrained by different material realities, asking different kinds of questions that permit different kinds of answers.

The simplification has pedagogical reality. It functions. Not because it’s comprehensive, but because it provides sufficient structure for novices to begin engaging with disciplinary modes of thought.

These consolidations are reductions. They smooth over debates that experts consider crucial. They present as unified what practitioners experience as fractured. They create provisional coherence where real disciplinary work is messier, more contested, more alive with disagreement.

The consolidation creates enough stability for practitioners to engage, and the engagement reveals where the consolidation falls short. The gap between framework and practice becomes a space for learning, not just about AI literacy but about the nature of disciplinary thinking itself.

t: Great Onboarding Makes People Feel as if They Belong Right Away
q: For newcomers, belonging is an entirely different experience from fitting in, feeling welcome, or being accepted. Belonging means the new team member is treated as an “insider” and they can be themselves by speaking candidly without the fear of rejection.

When new team members belong, they feel valued as a person, not just for the role they play or the skills they possess. Those who truly belong are remembered, included, and taken seriously. Their voice carries weight and can influence decisions.

As a rule, organizations are certainly apt to welcome or accept newcomers, but seldom work hard to make them feel that they are an integral part of the team from the get-go. Research shows that the sooner people feel they belong, the more likely they are to engage fully, commit to staying, and perform to their highest potential.

Instead of a highly structured process of acclimation, good organizations give new hires a menu of onboarding activities and let them choose what to prioritize (shadowing, process, product or service deep dives, organizational history, customer or client calls). By making the onboarding process somewhat self-directed, the organization signals that the new team member has instant influence over how things happen.

Belonging requires validation, so another best practice is to pair up new team members with other recent hires so they can share their integration stories. When newcomers learn how quickly others become an integral part of the organization, it bolsters their own sense of inclusion and attachment.

Lastly, leaders who want to create a sense of belonging with new hires assign them to a low-risk decision or improvement to show that they can shape the system. Those who truly belong can have immediate influence over others. This assignment demonstrates that.

Even in the workplace, people search for a place they can call home. When they find it, the organization benefits from a newfound loyalty and commitment. It’s up to leaders to create it. t: Ask Team Members to Create Their Own Goals

t: Nine AI Messages for Students
q: In my work I see a lot of uncritical celebration and shaming of people based on their AI use. Depending on your point of view, an AI enthusiast could be labeled innovative or immoral. An AI resistor could be labeled principled or out of touch. Using AI can be the right choice. Not using AI can also be the right choice.

Direct use is using AI to arrive at a solution as quickly as possible by asking it to complete a task for you. Collaborative use is using AI to assist you as you create work yourself. Anthropic found that about 50 percent of uses by college students were direct, and about 50 percent were collaborative.

If you are considering using AI for school, the most important question to ask yourself is, Am I investing in a process or am I just looking to generate a product? The former can deepen learning. The latter will not.

Chatbots have been designed to generate output quickly (a signal of fluency), deliver content with confidence (a signal of authority), take a responsive and sycophantic approach (a signal of care), and interact with us in natural, conversational language (a signal of humanity). These signals are cheap because they only make the chatbot appear fluent, authoritative, caring, and human so that we stay engaged with them.

AI is powerful, but it is not human. A LLM contains more information than your brain does, but it does not find that information meaningful. It can analyze patterns, make connections, and generate ideas faster than your brain might be able to, but it does not care about that work.

General purpose chatbots like ChatGPT would rather comfort you than warn you. They would rather keep you talking to them than encourage you to talk to a person. Their default mode is to endorse your ideas, not to question them.
Economics professor Jonathan Boymal puts it perfectly: You will not be replaced by AI, but by someone who has mastered their field deeply enough to take AI further than you can.

Recent surveys have found that while more than 80 percent of students have used AI for schoolwork, more than 50 percent of teachers have never used AI at all. What are we missing by not communicating across this gap?

Keeping the human in the loop has never been about inserting a person into a process that involves AI. It is about cultivating the kind of human who wants to be in the loop, who still feels the tug of curiosity, the satisfaction of an earned insight, the dignity of figuring something out.” Archived from Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Does My Organization Have So Many Meetings?
q: In far too many organizations, the stream of meetings is endless. They occur back-to-back and all day long. Instead of getting things done, people gather to discuss getting things done.

For every meeting that rightly serves to inform, update, and engage, there are other meetings where the primary purpose is to signal commitment, busyness, and status. When leaders do not take a hard stand against these unnecessary meetings, they propagate like weeds and can take over a culture.

Unknowingly, in many organizations, showcasing and discussing results becomes a substitute for productivity. This happens when talking about an issue begins to feel like making progress, and people lean into this perception.

Consequently, visibility and contribution in meetings become a highly prized and precious commodity. People who want to get ahead and prove their value naturally propose more meetings where they can showcase their talents.

The same is also true for organizations that fail to clarify decision rights. When people are unsure who owns a decision, they schedule a meeting to clarify it, usually without resolution. When everyone learns they are responsible, meetings become the default forum to discuss decisions without making them.
Leaders who lack trust in the team to execute independently also help meetings to multiply. To make themselves comfortable, these leaders call meetings to check in.

Meetings are time bandits that should be avoided whenever they can be. The unnecessary meetings that occur in any organization are hugely expensive (just think of the compensation, travel, and resource costs of everyone in the room) and undermine productivity.

Good leaders insist that every meeting be justified with a purpose, an agenda, and a decision goal. They examine recurring and standing meetings to determine if the reason they were created still exists. If not, they retire them.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Digital Detective Club: Teaching AI Literacy to Young Students
q: We're living through a profound shift in how text gets created. For the first time in history, our children will grow up in a world where much of what they read (homework help, explanations, stories, even personal messages) might be generated by AI rather than written by humans.

Most AI literacy curricula focus on older students: high schoolers learning about algorithmic bias, college students studying machine learning ethics. These are important, but they miss a critical window. By the time students reach high school, they've already spent years passively consuming AI-generated content without tools to evaluate it.

This curriculum is not about explaining how AI works under the hood (that can come later). Instead, it teaches elementary students (kindergarten through fifth grade) practical detective skills for the world they're actually living in.
This is not about demonizing AI. It's about building discernment. Children who complete this curriculum will not fear AI-generated text, but they will not blindly trust it either.

Students who cannot distinguish between human and AI writing will struggle to develop their own authentic voices. Students who cannot verify facts will be vulnerable to plausible-sounding misinformation. Students who never learn to demand sources will accept authority without question.

A student detective named Artyom discovered something important. He said: The robot makes English that is correct but not real. It's like textbook English. It follows all the rules perfectly, but it does not have the flavor of how people actually write.
Robot writing sounds nice but feels empty. Human stories have details that make them special and unique. Robot stories could belong to anyone.

Just because a robot sounds confident does not mean it's right. Your Job: Learn to check if facts are TRUE. Detective's Rule #1: If I cannot check it, I cannot trust it.” Archived from Educating AI (Nick Potkalitsky on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Research Bite #47: Features of Direct Instruction: Interactive Lessons
q: Direct Instruction programs only represent potential; teachers realise this through responsive interactions. Maximise active student responses to gain moment-to-moment data. Adjust pacing, corrections, and practice based on student performance to ensure mastery.

Teachers must understand that DI programs, while highly specified and scripted, only represent potential; their potential is only realised through the actual interactions that take place between teachers and students.

Teachers are comparable to actors in a Shakespearean play—they must present instructional formats with a range of expressivity, emphasis on key words and phrases, and controlled speed of speech. This ensures words are maximally comprehensible, supports correct responding, and helps motivate students.

Teachers must adjust their rate of speech and think time based on student responses. When the material is new or difficult, they must speak clearly and emphasise key words; when the material is easy or practised, they should speak more quickly to save time, keep students active and alert, and provide variety.

Teachers should skillfully use group unison vocal responses, which allow each student to respond to every question and enable the teacher to assess each student’s accuracy on each item, making group instruction efficient and powerful.

Individual turns should be used strategically to spot-check mastery, targeting items that caused errors or students who made errors. When giving individual turns, teachers should use the question/pause/name procedure to encourage covert engagement among students not selected to respond.

Prior to instruction, teachers must use placement tests and mastery tests to ensure students are grouped according to homogeneous skills and are placed at their precise instructional level. Correct placement prevents wasted time on mastered material, ensures students are challenged, and avoids frequent corrections that can lead to problem behaviour.
